newsitem.title: FINLAND: Key Finnish unions may go solo after ERM link.
newsitem.headline: Key Finnish unions may go solo after ERM link.

text.p: Finland's key export sector trade unions are likely to claim big nominal pay rises in the next wage talks as the markka was fixed to ERM at a level that will hurt industry's competitiveness, a union source said.
"We will start preparations to defend nominal earnings," the source, close to leaders of influential export industry unions, told Reuters on Saturday evening.
"Branch by branch, industrial unions, particularly in the export sector, will go out and take all they can get for themselves," he said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Initial union leader comments would be muted, he said.
"But I am saying now what they actually mean. And this will become evident as next autumn approaches," he said.
"We're kissing goodbye the chances of another centralised pay deal," he added, referring to the next scheduled round of collective bargaining due in autumn of 1997.
The government and the Bank of Finland decided on Saturday to link the markka to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism from Monday at a central parity rate of 3.04 markka per German mark.
"The competitiveness of Finnish industry has now been severely undermined," the union source said.
"If the ERM-link had been at 3.15 (markka per German mark) we could have survived," he said.

"The ERM link was more a political question of becoming presentable at court," he added, pointing at the government's stated objective to qualify for the third stage of Economic and Monetary Union due to start in 1999.

One year ago, unions and employers agreed on a nation-wide two-year centralised incomes settlement with modest pay rises. Thanks to income tax cuts, disposable earnings rose clearly in 1996 and are projected to rise further in 1997.

That deal was hailed by the government -- led by the Social Democratic Party with close union ties and including the equally labour-friendly Leftist Alliance -- as a triumph for its policy of active cooperation with the social partners.
But militant workers in export sector unions were less than pleased with the centralised deal's low nominal pay rises as 1995 corporate profits soared to record-highs.

The moderate wage hikes helped pave the way for low inflation and contributed to create the confidence in the economy, which has generated low interest rates and exchange rate stability, the government and the central bank have said.
In its statement on the link, the Bank of Finland said future pay rises should be moderate, too.

"Stability of the exchange rate requires that the economy follows a sustainable path of development. For Finland, this means especially that central government finances must be consolidated and that wage developments must continue on their moderate course," the Bank of Finland statement said.

But the union source said Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto's offer of further income tax cuts in 1998 in exchange for another centralised deal with low nominal pay rises now had scant chances of being approved by export sector unions.
